pos: n. (aromatic gums and drugs carried as merchandise)
etymology: From spice, through the Old French espicerie, the collective trade-word for aromatic wares. The Hebrew is nekoth, a word for the gum tragacanth or storax carried by caravan. It stands once in Scripture, in the sentence that sells Joseph.
biblical_def: The word appears one time, and it appears in the worst hour of Jacob's house: “And they sat down to eat bread: and they lifted up their eyes and looked, and, behold, a company of Ishmeelites came from Gilead with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt” (Genesis 37:25). The brothers have just thrown their brother into a pit, and they sit down to a meal. The caravan that crests the hill is a perfume caravan, and its cargo is named with a precision the narrative does not waste: spicery, balm, myrrh — the aromatics of healing, of burial, of worship. What the brothers did with that caravan is stated plainly: “Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt” (Genesis 37:28). The sweet-smelling freight and the sold brother go down the same road. Years later Jacob, not knowing whom he is sending to, orders the same goods as a present: “Take of the best fruits in the land in your vessels, and carry down the man a present, a little balm, and a little honey, spices, and myrrh, nuts, and almonds” (Genesis 43:11). The Psalmist gives the verdict over the whole affair: “He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant” (Psalm 105:17). God sent; the brothers sold. Both are true, and the spice caravan carried them both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spicery as spices in general; a repository of spices.
webster_full: SPICERY, n. Spices in general; also, a repository of spices.
SPICE, n. [Fr. epice.] A vegetable production, fragrant or aromatic to the smell, and pungent to the taste; used in sauces and in cookery, and also in medicine and embalming.
BALM, n. The sap or juice of trees or shrubs remarkably odoriferous or aromatic; that which heals or soothes.
MYRRH, n. A gum-resin issuing from the trunk and larger branches of a thorny shrub growing in Egypt and Arabia; used in embalming the dead.
CARAVAN, n. A company of travellers, pilgrims or merchants, marching or proceeding in a body over the deserts of Asia or Africa.
scriptures: Genesis 37:25

And they sat down to eat bread: and they lifted up their eyes and looked, and, behold, a company of Ishmeelites came from Gilead with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt.
Genesis 37:28
Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen ; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt.
Genesis 43:11

And their father Israel said unto them, If it must be so now, do this; take of the best fruits in the land in your vessels, and carry down the man a present, a little balm, and a little honey, spices, and myrrh, nuts, and almonds:
Psalm 105:17
He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant:
corruption_summary: The scene is read as a study in trauma and family dysfunction, which keeps the reader in the pit and never lets him see the throne the road was leading to.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern retelling of Genesis 37 is a case study in family dysfunction: a favoured child, resentful siblings, an unwise father, and a wound that shapes the rest of Joseph's life. Every element of that description is present in the text, and none of it is the point the text is making. Scripture does not present the sale as an injury Joseph must later process; it presents it as an errand God was running. Joseph himself says so to the men who sold him: what they meant unto evil, God meant unto good. The spice caravan was not an accident that Joseph survived. It was transport, and the God who governs the traffick of Gilead had booked the passage.

The second misreading is gentler and more common in the church: the sweetness of the cargo is turned into a devotional lesson about God bringing fragrance out of pain. The text is harder and better than that. The aromatics on those camels were the trade goods of healing and burial, and they were going down to Egypt whether Joseph went with them or not. Providence did not perfume the pit. It used a caravan that was already on the road, carrying goods already bought, driven by men with no interest in Jacob's family at all — and by that entirely ordinary commerce it set a man in Pharaoh's house so that a nation would eat. The doctrine here is not that suffering smells sweet. It is that nothing, not even a merchant's cargo manifest, lies outside the decree.

“A little balm, and a little honey, spices, and myrrh” — Jacob sends the same goods as a gift.

pos: v. (past tense of sew: joined with needle and thread)
etymology: From the Saxon siwian, to stitch. The word enters Scripture at the third chapter of Genesis and is the first manufacture recorded of fallen man — not a tool, not a shelter, but a covering.
biblical_def: The first thing sinners made, they made to hide: “And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons” (Genesis 3:7). The stitching is the point. Adam and Eve do not merely cover themselves; they manufacture a covering, and the covering is of their own devising, out of material at hand, addressing a shame they had just acquired. God's answer is not to praise the effort but to replace it: “Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them” (Genesis 3:21). Something died to clothe them, which the fig leaves had not required. The second appearance of the word is Job's, and it is mourning rather than concealment: “I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and defiled my horn in the dust” (Job 16:15). Job stitches the coarse cloth directly to the flesh; grief is worn, not draped. Between the two texts the whole doctrine of self-covering stands. Isaiah closes it: “But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away” (Isaiah 64:6). The best garment human hands can stitch is named, and it is rags.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sew as to unite or fasten together with a needle and thread.
webster_full: SEW, v.t. [Sax. siwian.] To unite or fasten together with a needle and thread.
SEWED, pp. United or fastened with a needle and thread.
APRON, n. A cloth or piece of leather worn on the fore part of the body, to keep the clothes clean.
SACKCLOTH, n. Cloth of which sacks are made; coarse cloth; worn in mourning and humiliation.
COVERING, n. That which covers; dress; vesture; anything spread over another.
scriptures: Genesis 3:7
And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.
Genesis 3:21
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.
I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and defiled my horn in the dust.
Isaiah 64:6
But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away.
corruption_summary: Self-covering is renamed self-improvement, and the fig leaf is recommended as the remedy rather than exposed as the problem.
corruption_paragraphs: Every religion that is not the gospel is a variation on sewing fig leaves. The material changes — moral effort, ritual observance, sincerity, good intentions, a life that on balance does more good than harm — but the operation is identical: the sinner takes what is nearest to hand, stitches it into a covering, and presents himself dressed. Scripture is not impressed by the workmanship. It notes only that the covering was self-made and that God removed it. The coats of skins are the first gospel picture in the Bible: God clothes, and to clothe He kills. What Adam sewed was not merely inadequate; it was the wrong kind of thing altogether.

The modern form of the error is therapeutic rather than religious. Shame is treated as a distortion in the self-image to be corrected by reassurance — the fig leaf is admired and reinforced, and the naked man is told he was never naked. Genesis will not permit it. The nakedness was real, the shame was the accurate perception of a real exposure, and the answer was neither to deny the exposure nor to improve the apron. It was a substitutionary covering given by God at the cost of a life. To tell a guilty conscience that its guilt is a misperception is to leave it in fig leaves in the presence of God.

“Did the LORD God make coats of skins” — the covering that cost a life.
“I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin” — Job stitches grief to the body.

etymology: From the Old French escurer, to cleanse by rubbing. In the law of the sin offering it is the required treatment of a brasen pot in which holy flesh has been boiled — the vessel that can be cleansed is cleansed, and the vessel that cannot is broken.
biblical_def: The word stands once, in a law about pots: “But the earthen vessel wherein it is sodden shall be broken: and if it be sodden in a brasen pot, it shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water” (Leviticus 6:28). The sin offering was most holy, and what touched it was affected by it: “Whatsoever shall touch the flesh thereof shall be holy: and when there is sprinkled of the blood thereof upon any garment, thou shalt wash that whereon it was sprinkled in the holy place” (Leviticus 6:27). A porous clay pot absorbs what is boiled in it and cannot be purged; it is destroyed. A brass pot is non-porous; it is scoured and rinsed and returns to service. The same principle governs the wider law of uncleanness: “And every earthen vessel, whereinto any of them falleth, whatsoever is in it shall be unclean; and ye shall break it” (Leviticus 11:33). The New Testament takes the vessel-image up and applies it to men: “If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work” (2 Timothy 2:21). Scouring is not a gentle word. It is abrasion applied until the surface is bright, and it is the Levitical picture of a sanctification that costs the vessel something.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scour as to rub hard with something rough, for the purpose of cleaning.
webster_full: SCOUR, v.t. To rub hard with something rough, for the purpose of cleaning; to make clean or bright.
SCOURED, pp. Rubbed with something rough for cleaning; cleansed; made bright.
RINSE, v.t. To wash; to cleanse by washing; to cleanse the inside by washing.
BRASS, n. An alloy of copper and zinc; in Scripture, generally copper or bronze, the metal of the altar and its vessels.
VESSEL, n. Any hollow utensil for holding liquors or other things; in Scripture, applied figuratively to persons.
scriptures: Leviticus 6:28
But the earthen vessel wherein it is sodden shall be broken: and if it be sodden in a brasen pot, it shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water.
Leviticus 6:27
Whatsoever shall touch the flesh thereof shall be holy: and when there is sprinkled of the blood thereof upon any garment, thou shalt wash that whereon it was sprinkled in the holy place.
Leviticus 11:33
And every earthen vessel, whereinto any of them falleth , whatsoever is in it shall be unclean; and ye shall break it.
2 Timothy 2:21
If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work.
corruption_summary: Sanctification is reimagined as acceptance of the vessel as it is, and the abrasive work Scripture describes is treated as damage rather than cleansing.
corruption_paragraphs: The law of the two pots is an unfashionable text because it insists on a distinction the age denies: some things can be cleansed and some must be destroyed. Modern religious sentiment prefers a universal solvent — everything is salvageable, nothing is broken past repair, and to speak of a vessel fit only for breaking is thought cruel. Leviticus is not cruel; it is exact. The earthen pot is broken not because God is severe but because clay holds what it has absorbed, and holiness is not served by pretending otherwise. The mercy in the chapter is that God tells His people which vessel is which rather than leaving them to guess.

The second corruption touches sanctification directly. Scouring is friction; it removes material. When the New Testament says purge himself, it describes a man taking abrasive action against what is in him, and the church has largely exchanged that language for the vocabulary of self-acceptance. A vessel unto honour, in Paul's sentence, is not a vessel that has learned to think well of itself; it is a vessel that has been scoured. The Reformed doctrine of progressive sanctification keeps both halves together: the vessel is chosen and set apart by grace alone, and the vessel is scoured, daily, all its life, by the Spirit working through the means God appointed.

Hebrew shataph (H7857) — to rinse, flood, overflow; the second half of the treatment.

Hebrew nechosheth (H5178) — brass, copper, bronze; the vessel that may be scoured.
Greek ekkathairo (G1571) — to purge out thoroughly; 2 Timothy 2:21, purge himself.
usage: “It shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water” — the brass pot returns to service.
“Ye shall break it” — the clay pot that cannot be purged.
“A vessel unto honour, sanctified” — Paul applies the vessel-law to men.

pos: n. pl. (the gold settings that held the stones of the high priest's breastplate)
etymology: From enclose, to shut in. The Hebrew mishbetsah means a woven or braided setting — the filigree of gold into which each stone was fixed. The margin of Exodus 28 renders the word fillings, because the stone fills the socket prepared for it.
biblical_def: Twelve stones were set in the breastplate of the high priest, and the sockets that held them have their own name: “And the fourth row a beryl, and an onyx, and a jasper: they shall be set in gold in their inclosings” (Exodus 28:20). When the work was executed, the same word records that it was done as commanded: “And the fourth row, a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper: they were inclosed in ouches of gold in their inclosings” (Exodus 39:13). The detail matters because of what the stones were: “And the stones shall be with the names of the children of Israel, twelve, according to their names, like the engravings of a signet; every one with his name shall they be according to the twelve tribes” (Exodus 28:21). Each tribe had a stone, each stone had a name cut into it, and each named stone had a gold socket made to fit it and no other. Aaron wore the tribes over his heart into the holy place, and none of them could fall out. The LORD later uses the same imagery of His own people: “And they shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels; and I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him” (Malachi 3:17). The inclosing is the doctrine of preservation rendered in goldsmith's work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inclose as to surround; to shut in; to encompass; and an inclosure as that which is inclosed or surrounded.
webster_full: INCLOSE, v.t. To surround; to shut in; to confine on all sides; to encompass.
INCLOSURE, n. The act of inclosing; the separation of land from common ground; that which is inclosed.
OUCH, n. A socket or bezel in which a precious stone is set; the setting of a jewel.
BREASTPLATE, n. Armor for the breast; in Jewish antiquity, a folded piece of the rich embroidered stuff of the ephod, set with twelve precious stones.
SIGNET, n. A seal; particularly, the seal used by a sovereign in sealing private letters and grants.
scriptures: Exodus 28:20
And the fourth row a beryl, and an onyx, and a jasper: they shall be set in gold in their inclosings.
Exodus 39:13
And the fourth row, a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper: they were inclosed in ouches of gold in their inclosings.
Exodus 28:21

And the stones shall be with the names of the children of Israel, twelve , according to their names, like the engravings of a signet; every one with his name shall they be according to the twelve tribes.
Malachi 3:17
And they shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels; and I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him.
corruption_summary: The tabernacle's exactness is treated as priestly fussiness rather than as revelation, and the doctrine of preservation it pictures is exchanged for a security the believer must maintain himself.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the minute specifications of the sanctuary are revelation, not inventory. A generation trained to skim Exodus 28 for the interesting parts loses the argument the chapter is making: that God designed a socket for every stone, named every tribe, and required the goldsmith to make the setting fit the stone rather than the stone fit the setting. The book of Hebrews reasons from precisely such details, and a church that cannot be bothered with inclosings will not follow the argument when it reaches the Antitype.

There is a live misuse worth naming. The breastplate is often preached as a picture of how precious the believer is to God, which is true, and then stopped there, which is sentimental. The stones were not in the sockets because of anything in the stones; they were cut, named, and fixed by another, and carried by a priest who was not one of them. What the inclosing guarantees is not the worth of the jewel but the reliability of the setting. The Reformed doctrine of the perseverance of the saints says the same thing in plainer speech: those whom God has set, He keeps, and the security lies in the goldsmith's work and in the High Priest who wears it, never in the stone.

“They were inclosed in ouches of gold” — the command executed exactly.
“When I make up my jewels” — the LORD claims the stones as His own.

pos: adj. (of a vine, left unpruned and untended)
etymology: From un- + dress, in the old agricultural sense of dressing a vine — pruning, propping, and tending it. To leave a vine undressed is not neglect but obedience: it is what the sabbath of the land required.
biblical_def: The word belongs to the law of the sabbath year, and it commands a farmer to stop farming: “That which groweth of its own accord of thy harvest thou shalt not reap, neither gather the grapes of thy vine undressed: for it is a year of rest unto the land” (Leviticus 25:5). A vine left undressed is a vine not pruned, not trained, not worked. Every instinct of husbandry protests, and the law overrules the instinct for one year in seven. The same command governs the fiftieth year: “A jubile shall that fiftieth year be unto you: ye shall not sow, neither reap that which groweth of itself in it, nor gather the grapes in it of thy vine undressed” (Leviticus 25:11). The obvious objection is raised in the text itself, and God answers it before it can become unbelief: “And if ye shall say, What shall we eat the seventh year? behold, we shall not sow, nor gather in our increase” (Leviticus 25:20), to which the reply is a promise of a threefold harvest in the sixth year. The reason underneath the whole statute is a matter of title: “The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Leviticus 25:23). The undressed vine is a confession. It says the field belongs to God and the tenant can afford to take his hands off it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to dress a vine as to prune, trim and cultivate it; undressed is therefore untrimmed and uncultivated.
webster_full: UNDRESSED, a. Not dressed; not pruned or trimmed, as a vine; not cultivated.
DRESS, v.t. To prune; to trim; to cultivate; as, to dress a vine; to dress a field.
VINE, n. The plant which produces grapes; a climbing or trailing plant.
SABBATH, n. A day of rest; the sabbath of the land, a year of rest appointed to the Israelites.
JUBILEE, n. Among the Israelites, every fiftieth year, in which lands reverted to their former owners and slaves were set free.
scriptures: Leviticus 25:5
That which groweth of its own accord of thy harvest thou shalt not reap, neither gather the grapes of thy vine undressed: for it is a year of rest unto the land.
Leviticus 25:11
A jubile shall that fiftieth year be unto you: ye shall not sow, neither reap that which groweth of itself in it, nor gather the grapes in it of thy vine undressed.
Leviticus 25:20
And if ye shall say, What shall we eat the seventh year? behold, we shall not sow, nor gather in our increase:
Leviticus 25:23
The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me.
corruption_summary: The sabbath of the land is reassigned to environmental stewardship as its primary meaning, and the statute's actual argument — that the land is God's and the farmer is a tenant — is left out.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 25 is now most often cited as an early conservation ordinance: let the soil rest, rotate the ground, do not exhaust the earth. Sound agriculture may well follow from the statute, but the chapter gives a different reason and gives it explicitly. The land is mine, says the LORD; ye are strangers and sojourners with me. The sabbath year is a property claim before it is an agricultural practice, and the undressed vine is the visible sign of the claim. To reduce it to stewardship of resources is to keep the ecology and lose the landlord.

The harder edge of the law is what it demands of faith. A farmer who does not prune in the seventh year has no harvest in the seventh year, and the text puts his objection into words — what shall we eat? — rather than shaming him for raising it. God answers with a promise of provision in the sixth year, which means the obedience of the seventh rests entirely on whether the farmer believed the promise twelve months earlier. That is the ordinary shape of faith in Scripture: a present act of obedience grounded on a word already spoken. The vine standing undressed in the sun is what belief looks like when it has been planted in dirt.

“What shall we eat the seventh year?” — the objection God states and answers.
“The land is mine” — the reason under the whole statute.

etymology: From the Greek kuparissos, through the Latin cupressus. The Hebrew tirzah occurs once. It is named in Isaiah's account of how an idol is manufactured, standing between the cedar and the oak in the carpenter's choice of stock.
biblical_def: The word stands once, and it stands in the middle of the most devastating description of idol-making in Scripture: “He heweth him down cedars, and taketh the cypress and the oak, which he strengtheneth for himself among the trees of the forest: he planteth an ash, and the rain doth nourish it” (Isaiah 44:14). Isaiah is deliberately slow here. He follows the timber from the seedling that God's own rain waters, through the felling, to the workshop, and he will not let the reader skip a step, because every step indicts the workman. The same log serves two purposes: “Then shall it be for a man to burn: for he will take thereof, and warm himself; yea, he kindleth it, and baketh bread; yea, he maketh a god, and worshippeth it; he maketh it a graven image, and falleth down thereto” (Isaiah 44:15). Half the tree cooks his dinner; the other half receives his prayers. The prophet then records the prayer itself: “And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god” (Isaiah 44:17). The poor man's version is described with the same irony: “He that is so impoverished that he hath no oblation chooseth a tree that will not rot; he seeketh unto him a cunning workman to prepare a graven image, that shall not be moved” (Isaiah 40:20). Cypress was chosen because it lasts. That is the whole argument the idolater has.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cypress as a genus of trees, the wood of which is remarkably durable, and the tree an emblem of mourning.
webster_full: CYPRESS, n. A genus of trees, the wood of which is very durable; the branches were formerly used at funerals, hence it is an emblem of mourning.
CEDAR, n. A large evergreen tree of the genus Juniperus or Pinus, valuable for its durable timber.
OAK, n. A tree of the genus Quercus, of great strength and durability.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
GRAVEN, pp. Carved; engraved; cut, as an image, in wood, stone or metal.
scriptures: Isaiah 44:14
He heweth him down cedars, and taketh the cypress and the oak, which he strengtheneth for himself among the trees of the forest: he planteth an ash, and the rain doth nourish it.
Isaiah 44:15

Then shall it be for a man to burn: for he will take thereof, and warm himself; yea, he kindleth it, and baketh bread; yea, he maketh a god, and worshippeth it; he maketh it a graven image, and falleth down thereto.
Isaiah 44:17
And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god.
Isaiah 40:20
He that is so impoverished that he hath no oblation chooseth a tree that will not rot; he seeketh unto him a cunning workman to prepare a graven image, that shall not be moved.
corruption_summary: Idolatry is redefined as a primitive stage of religion outgrown by modern man, which conceals the fact that Isaiah's workman is a sophisticate reasoning about durable materials.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern treatment of Isaiah 44 files it under the religion of the ancient Near East and leaves it there: people once believed statues were alive, and we no longer do, so the chapter has antiquarian interest only. This misses Isaiah's actual charge. His idolater is not a credulous primitive; he is a man making reasonable decisions about timber. He selects cypress because cypress resists rot. He hires a cunning workman. He is attentive, practical, and economical — and at the end of an entirely rational process he addresses a piece of wood as my god. The prophet's point is that idolatry is not a failure of intelligence but a corruption of the heart, which is why intelligence never cures it.

The second corruption is a churchly one. Because the passage mocks carved images, Protestants have often read it as a text about other people, finished business, a sin the Reformation settled. Calvin's judgment is the sounder one: the human heart is a perpetual factory of idols, and it does not require a workshop. What Isaiah exposes is the mechanism — taking something God made and given, dividing it, and assigning to one part of it the trust that belongs to God alone. A career, a family, a reputation, a doctrine of one's own devising, each can be the residue of the log. The material has changed; the transaction is identical.

pos: n. pl. (the small shoots at the top of a tree)
etymology: From the Saxon twig, a small shoot, akin to twa, two, from the forking of a branch. Ezekiel uses the word twice, both times of the tender top of a cedar — once cropped off by an eagle in judgment, once cropped off by the LORD in promise.
biblical_def: Ezekiel's riddle of the two eagles turns on a handful of shoots. The first eagle is Babylon: “He cropped off the top of his young twigs, and carried it into a land of traffick; he set it in a city of merchants” (Ezekiel 17:4). The cropping is the deportation of Jehoiachin and the royal house to Babylon — a violent act performed by a foreign power for its own commercial ends. Then, at the end of the chapter, the identical gesture is made by another hand: “Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent” (Ezekiel 17:22). What Babylon did for plunder, God does for planting. The result is not a trading post but a kingdom: “In the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it: and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell” (Ezekiel 17:23). And the chapter closes by naming who is sovereign over every tree in the field: “And all the trees of the field shall know that I the LORD have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish: I the LORD have spoken and have done it” (Ezekiel 17:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines twig as a small shoot or branch of a tree or other plant, of no definite length or size.
webster_full: TWIG, n. [Sax. twig.] A small shoot or branch of a tree or other plant, of no definite length or size.
BRANCH, n. A shoot, or arm of a tree; the offspring of a family; in Scripture, a title of the Messiah.
CROP, v.t. To cut off the ends of anything; to pull off; to pluck.
CEDAR, n. A large evergreen tree valuable for its durable and fragrant timber.
PLANT, v.t. To put into the ground and cover, as seed for growth; to set in the ground for growth; to settle; to establish.
scriptures: Ezekiel 17:4
He cropped off the top of his young twigs, and carried it into a land of traffick; he set it in a city of merchants.
Ezekiel 17:22

Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent:
Ezekiel 17:23

In the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it: and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell.
Ezekiel 17:24

And all the trees of the field shall know that I the LORD have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish: I the LORD have spoken and have done it.
corruption_summary: The chapter is flattened into ancient political commentary, and the Messianic promise at its end is treated as a hopeful coda rather than the point the riddle was built to reach.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 17 is commonly handled as a coded editorial on sixth-century foreign policy: Zedekiah broke his oath to Nebuchadnezzar, sought Egyptian help, and was destroyed. All of that is in the chapter and is meant to be. But the historical-critical instinct to stop at the political layer removes the chapter's architecture. The riddle is constructed so that the same verb falls twice — an eagle crops a twig, and then the Lord GOD crops a twig — and the second cropping is the answer to the first. To read only the politics is to hear the question and walk out before the reply.

The tender twig planted on the high mountain of Israel, becoming a goodly cedar sheltering every wing, is Messianic, and the Reformed reading has always said so. What corrupts the passage is not usually a denial of that but a dilution of it: the promise is generalized into an assurance that history bends toward restoration. Ezekiel is more particular. A specific shoot is taken from a specific house by a specific hand and planted in a specific place, and the trees of the field learn from it who brings down and who exalts. The comfort of verse 24 is not that things improve; it is that the LORD has spoken and has done it.

“I the LORD have spoken and have done it” — the seal on the riddle.

pos: n. pl. (small shoots or sprays put forth by a vine or tree)
etymology: Of Northern origin, akin to the Saxon sprec, a shoot. Scripture uses it twice, both times of growth that is about to be cut — the sprigs of Isaiah's vineyard taken off with pruning hooks, and the sprigs of Ezekiel's low vine.
biblical_def: Isaiah sets the word in a harvest that never comes: “For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away and cut down the branches” (Isaiah 18:5). The timing is the severity. The cutting falls not on a barren plant but on one that is doing everything a plant should — budding, flowering, setting fruit — and it falls before the harvest, so that all the promise of the season is removed at the moment it is most visible. Ezekiel uses the word of a vine deliberately kept small: “And it grew, and became a spreading vine of low stature, whose branches turned toward him, and the roots thereof were under him: so it became a vine, and brought forth branches, and shot forth sprigs” (Ezekiel 17:6). It is a real vine and it really grows, but it grows toward the wrong sovereign. The Lord Jesus takes up the same husbandry and gives the rule that governs it: “Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit” (John 15:2). And He states the end of the shoot that is merely attached: “If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned” (John 15:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sprig as a shoot, twig or small branch; a spray.
webster_full: SPRIG, n. A small shoot or twig of a tree or other plant; a spray.
PRUNE, v.t. To lop or cut off the superfluous branches of trees, to make them bear better fruit or grow higher.
PRUNING-HOOK, n. An instrument used in pruning trees, having a hooked or curved blade.
VINE, n. The plant which produces grapes; a climbing or trailing plant.
HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground; one who labors in tillage.
scriptures: Isaiah 18:5
For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away and cut down the branches.
Ezekiel 17:6

And it grew, and became a spreading vine of low stature, whose branches turned toward him, and the roots thereof were under him: so it became a vine, and brought forth branches, and shot forth sprigs.
John 15:2
Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.
John 15:6
If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned.
corruption_summary: Pruning is recast as a gentle metaphor for personal growth, and the cutting off of fruitless branches is quietly dropped from the vineyard.
corruption_paragraphs: John 15 is preached constantly and halved routinely. The purging of the fruitful branch survives, softened into the reassurance that difficulty is God improving us. The first clause of the verse — every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away — is passed over, and with it the seriousness that makes the second clause a comfort rather than a platitude. Isaiah's picture is the necessary corrective: the sprigs were cut with pruning hooks before the harvest, while the bud was perfect. God's husbandry is not sentimental about promise. It is interested in fruit.

The second corruption is the confusion of attachment with abiding. Ezekiel's vine of low stature grew, spread, and shot forth sprigs; by every visible measure it was alive, and it was planted by a gardener whose purpose it served rather than God's. Our Lord draws the same distinction between the branch that is in me and bears, and the man who does not abide and is gathered for burning. The doctrine the church needs here is the one the Reformed confessions state plainly: outward membership in the visible vine is not union with Christ, and the difference between the two is not visible in the spring. It is visible at harvest.

Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, remain; the condition of fruitfulness in John 15.
usage: “He shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks” — cutting before the harvest.
“Shot forth sprigs” — a vine that grows toward the wrong king.
“He purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit” — the husbandman's purpose.

pos: n. (the stock or trunk of a tree, especially one cut down)
etymology: From the Saxon stemn, a stock or trunk. The Hebrew geza means a stump — what is left standing when a tree has been felled. It occurs once in this form, and it carries the Messianic promise of Isaiah 11.
biblical_def: One verse holds the word, and it is among the greatest in the prophets: “And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isaiah 11:1). The force of the sentence is in the word stem. It is not a tree; it is a stump. The house of David, by the time Isaiah has finished with Ahaz, is a felled thing — cut down to the ground, its royal line reduced to a stub in the soil, and named here not by the king's name but by his father's, Jesse of Bethlehem, as though the monarchy were being taken back to the farm it came from. Out of that stump a shoot comes. What rests on the shoot is stated next: “And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:2). The reach of His kingdom follows: “And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious” (Isaiah 11:10). Paul cites that very line as the warrant for the Gentile mission: “And again, Esaias saith, There shall be a root of Jesse, and he that shall rise to reign over the Gentiles; in him shall the Gentiles trust” (Romans 15:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stem as the principal body of a tree, shrub or plant; the stock; the race or family.
webster_full: STEM, n. [Sax. stemn.] The principal body of a tree, shrub or plant; the stock; the firm part which supports the branches.
STEM, n. The stock of a family; race; generation; as, a noble stem.
ROD, n. A twig or shoot; a branch; also, an instrument of correction, and a badge of authority.
BRANCH, n. The shoot of a tree; in Scripture, an appellation of the Messiah, Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5.
ENSIGN, n. The flag or banner of a military band; a standard set up as a signal of gathering.
scriptures: Isaiah 11:1
And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots:
Isaiah 11:2
And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD;
Isaiah 11:10
And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious.
Romans 15:12
And again, Esaias saith, There shall be a root of Jesse, and he that shall rise to reign over the Gentiles; in him shall the Gentiles trust.
corruption_summary: The prophecy is reassigned to a purely eighth-century hope for a better Judean king, and the stump is turned into a metaphor for national resilience.
corruption_paragraphs: The historical-critical reading confines Isaiah 11 to its own century: the prophet hopes for a righteous Davidic successor, perhaps Hezekiah, and the language is court rhetoric of a familiar Near Eastern kind. The dictionary rejects this reading and follows the apostle. Paul quotes verse 10 in Romans 15:12 as a prophecy of Christ's reign over the Gentiles, and the New Testament's use of the Old is the authoritative use. A prophecy that terminates on Hezekiah cannot bear the weight of verses 6 through 9, and no Judean king ever did.

A softer corruption preaches the stump as a lesson in resilience — nations and people can be cut down and still come back. The text says the opposite about the stump. A stump cannot come back; that is what makes it a stump. The whole point of naming Jesse rather than David is that the royal house had been reduced to the obscurity it started in, and that nothing in the wood accounts for the shoot. The rod comes forth because God promised it would, and the Spirit rests on Him because the Father gives Him the Spirit without measure. The doctrine is sovereign grace, not natural recovery.

“The spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him” — the anointing of the shoot.
“To it shall the Gentiles seek” — the reach Paul claims for the gospel.

etymology: From shade, Saxon scead. The word occurs twice, both in the LORD's description of behemoth, where the greatest of the beasts is found lying down in the covert of the trees.
biblical_def: Out of the whirlwind God describes a creature and where it rests: “He lieth under the shady trees, in the covert of the reed, and fens” (Job 40:21). The picture is repeated in the next verse with the shade doing the work: “The shady trees cover him with their shadow; the willows of the brook compass him about” (Job 40:22). The point of the whole speech is stated at its head: “Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox” (Job 40:15). God is not describing the beast to frighten Job but to enlarge him. The creature is enormous, entirely beyond Job's management, and it spends its day lying in shade God provided, eating grass God grew. Job has been demanding an account of the government of the world, and the LORD answers by walking him past an animal he has never had to feed. The same shade is elsewhere the standing figure of God's own protection: “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1). Shade in Scripture is never merely scenery. It is a picture of covering given from above to a creature that cannot make its own.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shady as abounding with shade; sheltered from the rays of the sun.
webster_full: SHADY, a. Abounding with shade or shades; causing shade; sheltered from the rays of the sun.
SHADE, n. Obscurity caused by the interception of light; shelter from the direct rays of the sun.
COVERT, n. A shelter; a defense; a thicket; a hiding place.
FEN, n. Low land overflowed, or covered wholly or partially with water, but producing sedge, coarse grasses or other aquatic plants; a marsh.
WILLOW, n. A tree of the genus Salix, growing commonly by watercourses.
scriptures: He lieth under the shady trees, in the covert of the reed, and fens.
The shady trees cover him with their shadow; the willows of the brook compass him about.
Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox.
Psalm 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
corruption_summary: The speeches from the whirlwind are read as God evading Job's question, when they are in fact the answer — delivered in creatures rather than propositions.
corruption_paragraphs: A common modern reading treats Job 38 through 41 as a magnificent non-answer: Job asks why he suffers, and God replies with a tour of the animal kingdom and never addresses the question. That reading assumes the only satisfying answer would be an explanation. Scripture's premise is different. Job's trouble was not a missing datum but a shrunken view of God, and the LORD corrects it by enlarging the view — the wild ass, the ostrich, the war horse, behemoth lying under the shady trees. A God who feeds what Job cannot even approach is a God who may be trusted with what Job cannot understand.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is that the creation speeches are pastoral, not merely poetic. The shade over behemoth is real shade, provided by real trees, for a real beast who did not plant them. Job is being taught the doctrine of providence in a form he cannot argue with. When he answers at last, he does not say he now understands his suffering; he says he had heard of God by the hearing of the ear, and now his eye seeth Him. That is what the whirlwind was for.
